newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel faces hurdles on road to privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Israel faces hurdles on road to privatisation.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to put life back into Israel's moribund privatisation programme, but selling key state enterprises will be a difficult task, analysts said on Thursday.

"I hope they will succeed, but it was a big tactical and operative mistake to raise expectations so much," said Yossi Nitzani, managing director of Capital Market Models and director of the Government Corporations Authority from 1991 until 1995.
He said the government threatened the credibility of the privatisation effort if it failed to execute the programme.

On Wednesday, the government unveiled its long-awaited programme. The plan calls for selling shares in Bezeq Israel Telecom, Israel Chemicals Ltd, Zim Israel Navigation and a host of smaller companies this year.

Others, like El Al airlines and Industrial Development Bank, require further preparatory work and will likely be sold only in 1998 at the earliest. Officials said they would also be merging and closing smaller companies or selling their assets.
The plan, however, does not include specific recommendations of when, how or how much of any company to privatise.

Officials acknowledged some of the difficulties involved in privatising but said they were determined to go ahead with the programme, even if it meant the government might have to sell some companies at low valuations.

"I think we are more determined (than governments in the past) to undertake measures and I believe we will do it -- but not over one year, rather over several years," said Moshe Leon, Netanyahu's adviser on economic affairs.

The plan does not include the state-owned banks, whose sale is being conducted by the Treasury, nor does it include a number of major state-owned companies, like Israel Electric Corp and Oil Refineries Ltd.
Indeed, Leon said most of the $1.3 billion the government hopes to raise this year from privatisation would come from bank sales not from government companies.
In trying to privatise the government companies officials face an array of obstacles.

Israel Chemicals and Zim are controlled by the industrialist Shoul Eisenberg through Israel Corp, while Britain's Cable & Wireless holds 10 percent of Bezeq. In all three companies the government has to reach an agreement with its partners on how to proceed with share sales, which in the past has proven difficult, analysts said.

Amnon Mandelbaum, of Poalim Capital Markets, said the government should learn from past mistakes and sell off its entire holdings in a single company at one time. He said the government would be able to hasten privatisation by selling its stakes through private sales rather than public placements, which Leon said was its preferred route.
The Israeli capital market is showing signs of climbing out of its three-year slump, but analysts doubt it is ready to absorb big public offerings.
"I would wait a few more months. Valuations and demand are still low," said a foreign investment banker. "They are probably better off selling the big companies in the international markets."
But overseas, not all the big companies being proposed for privatisation would be greeted enthusiastically by investors.
"It (privatisation) will very much depend on industry specifics and company specifics," said the foreign banker. "If you look at shipping, there's not much interest from investors worldwide."

"Bezeq is in an attractive sector, but it's going to have hard times ahead of it," the investment banker said. "There's a lot of appetite for telecoms issues. It's a sector that will still be hot in 1997."
Bezeq is facing new competitive challenges in the next few years in international, interurban and local phone service, as well as stepped-up competition in cellular telephones.

Leon said that in some sectors the government planned to undertake liberalisation measures before privatising, which will also cause delays. Tsipi Livni, director of the Government Corporations Authority, said Israel had learned from Britain's experience not to try to privatise monopolies, like the Electric Corporation.
Nitzani said he did not doubt the government's commitment to privatisation but said those responsible for implementing do not fully understand the complications in privatising companies.
"I am convinced they really want to do it," he said. "The programme is somewhat overblown because they don't understand the territory."
